data.title: Indonesia revokes Riau forestry permits held by APRIL Group unit over peatland fires, violations
data.description:
[JAKARTA] Indonesia has revoked forestry permits covering 338,536 hectares (ha) held by Riau Andalan Pulp and Paper (RAPP), a subsidiary of Asia Pacific Resources International Limited (APRIL) Group.

The move, which affects an area about 4.5 times the size of Singapore, was taken over alleged environmental violations, including recurring peatland fires, illegal plantations and damage to protected areas, the government’s forest enforcement task force said on Friday (Nov 20).

The enforcement push comes amid heightened scrutiny of companies linked to forest fires and transboundary haze; the latest move marks a significant crackdown on major corporate players in the forestry sector.

The permits were revoked under a Forestry Ministerial Decree dated Thursday (Nov 19), with the entire concession area in Riau province returning to state control, said the Forest Area Enforcement Task Force, known as Satgas PKH, in a statement on Friday.

“All activities within the revoked concession areas have been halted, while the government has taken back control of the land,” it added. “The revocation does not absolve the company of its environmental restoration obligations or potential legal liabilities.”

The task force cited recurring peatland fires, oil palm plantations spanning 18,362.74 ha, unauthorised mining activities covering 541.46 ha, and damage to protected areas spanning 211.54 ha as grounds for the revocation.

It also raised concerns over the protection of areas surrounding Tesso Nilo National Park, which provides habitat for endangered Sumatran elephants.

APRIL Group said it learnt about the government’s decision through media reports. It added that it was awaiting formal notification and further clarification from authorities.

“We respect the authority of the government and will continue to communicate constructively with the relevant authorities,” the company said in a statement. It added that it would respond through the appropriate channels once it received formal notification.

RAPP said that responsible forest management is central to its operations, adding that it manages industrial plantations while conserving forest areas and supporting peatland restoration initiatives.

The company said its immediate priority is to safeguard the welfare of communities dependent on its operations, as well as to minimise disruption to contractors, customers, suppliers and other business partners.

RAPP, which has operated in Riau for more than three decades, is a major producer of pulp and paper products. Its operations are centred around Pangkalan Kerinci in Pelalawan regency, where its industrial complex has helped drive the development of the surrounding town.

The company is part of APRIL Group, a pulp, paper and forestry business owned by Indonesian conglomerate Royal Golden Eagle, founded by billionaire Sukanto Tanoto.

The group produces fibre-based products for customers in more than 100 markets worldwide, with more than 85 per cent of its output exported, according to the company.

Broader forest enforcement

Indonesian authorities have stepped up investigations into suspected corporate involvement in forest and land fires, as transboundary haze from the blazes has spread to neighbouring countries, raising regional concerns over air quality.

The haze also prompted Singapore authorities to step up enforcement.

The National Environment Agency in October issued preventive measure notices to 10 companies in Indonesia, and notices seeking information from 10 Singapore-based companies.

On Nov 4, Singapore passed sweeping changes to its haze law, which will increase financial penalties and allow restrictions on business dealings with certain companies.

Established by Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto, Satgas PKH was formed as part of the government’s sweeping crackdown on the illegal exploitation of forest areas, tasked with reclaiming land encroached upon for commercial activities and restoring state control over forest assets.

The task force took action against another company in Riau, Gemilang Sawit Lestari, after finding indications that its non-estate palm oil mill in Kuantan Singingi regency bought and processed palm oil sourced from plantations operating illegally inside forest areas.

Authorities said the mill’s operations may have encouraged further encroachment into surrounding forests.

The task force recommended rejecting the company’s pending application to release about 32 ha of forest land and reclaiming the area.

data.title: No free lunch: South-east Asiaâs price controls become harder to sustain
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] At supermarket counters from Kuala Lumpur to Manila, global macroeconomic shocks have been jacking up grocery bills – while extracting much higher costs from many governments.

In much of South-east Asia, food carries a significant weight in the consumer price index basket. The prolonged shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz has pushed up global oil prices, in turn raising transportation, logistics and production costs. Higher fertiliser prices have also made agricultural production costlier, while El Nino-related weather conditions have hit crop yields.

But these cost increases have not uniformly translated to higher consumer prices at the till – partly because some governments have stepped in to cap prices or offer subsidies.

Can they afford to keep intervening to protect household purchasing power?

Established caps

“Countries with larger buffers, stronger currencies or diversified import sources can absorb more of the shock,” says Maybank analyst Brian Lee. “Countries with thin inventories or greater import dependence are considerably more exposed.”

Food prices in the Philippines rose by 6.4 per cent year on year in October, down slightly from inflation of 6.8 per cent in September. Yet rice prices in the country – which produces more than 70 per cent of its rice supply domestically – still picked up at a faster clip.

Food has been a key driver of headline inflation in the Philippines. Catharine Kho, a senior economist at the Asean+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (Amro), notes that heavy rains and flooding disrupted production and deliveries recently, while “higher fuel costs and a weaker peso added to these pressures”.

That’s even though countries such as the Philippines and Indonesia have stockpiles of staples such as rice to serve as what Amro economist Ravisara Hataiseree calls “strategic food reserves… to buffer against sudden supply disruptions”.

At the same time, another factor determining the extent of cost pass-through in developing economies has been state controls on the prices of staples.

Price controls are well established in the region, where policymakers favour mandatory price ceilings for providing immediate and highly visible relief to keep essential goods affordable, while subsidies are preferred for preserving the incentive to produce or supply goods.

As Lee points out: “For staples such as rice, sugar and cooking oil, governments are more inclined to intervene because consumption is widespread, these goods carry high social and political salience, and poorer households spend a larger share of their income on them.”

RHB group chief economist Barnabas Gan comments that food inflation in Malaysia has “remained relatively contained compared to what would otherwise have been expected”, thanks in part to its price controls on a range of grocery staples.

Notably, Malaysia has capped the price of standard coarse white sugar at RM2.85 (US$0.70) per kilogram since 2018. This is among the lowest prices in the region, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence economists Ahmad Mobeen, Lei Yi and Harumi Taguchi, who highlight Malaysia’s “longstanding system of administered prices”.

While direct consumer subsidies for sugar were abolished in 2013, Malaysia has offered incentives to sugar refiners since late 2023, to maintain retail price stability.

Responsive rollouts

Beyond long-running schemes, governments may also step in on an ad-hoc basis to manage prices – such as the Philippines’ imposition, in May, of a 50-peso (US$0.79) ceiling on certain rice imports for 30 days.

In response to the weather-related production declines, the Indonesian government in early November announced that it would distribute one million tonnes of rice through its existing Food Supply and Price Stabilisation programme at 12,500 rupiah (US$0.68) per kilogram, below the market rate of between 15,000 and 17,000 rupiah per kilogram.

Established schemes to tackle fuel costs – another common target of government price controls – have taken on increased prominence in the wake of the global energy shock too.

For instance, Thailand has an oil fuel fund that the government taps to compensate for the increase in retail fuel prices when oil prices surge.

Nomura chief Asean economist Euben Paracuelles sees a sharp divergence in energy price increases across South-east Asian states depending on whether they maintain fuel subsidies.

Malaysia uses subsidies to maintain RON95 fuel prices at RM1.99 per litre for eligible residents, while Indonesia keeps subsidised prices for RON90 petrol at 10,000 rupiah per litre and for biodiesel blend at 6,800 rupiah per litre.

Such fuel subsidies have been effective in curbing inflation, with levels within authorities’ target ranges, Paracuelles says.

He pointed out that Malaysia and Indonesia have seen zero increase in subsidised retail fuel prices since the global energy crisis began with the outbreak of hostilities in the Middle East in February. 

At the opposite extreme, the Philippines has no measures to tackle fuel price changes – “so the pass-through is quick and very large”, he said, with 50 to 60 per cent jumps in retail fuel prices in the same period.

Such moves come as more than 80 per cent of Asia-Pacific economies have introduced measures to dampen the pass-through of higher energy prices since February, according to an October regional assessment by the International Monetary Fund.

Conversely, Singapore manages inflation through an exchange rate-based monetary policy and direct household support in the form of vouchers, rebates and payouts. The government explicitly avoids enforcing price ceilings or subsidies to prevent market distortions.

But the National Trades Union Congress-affiliated FairPrice Group (FPG) implements voluntary, time-limited price freezes and discounts on daily essentials. In October, it lowered prices for chicken and eggs – two popular protein staples – until the end of 2026.

In all, FPG has committed more than S$7.5 million worth of savings on groceries and household essentials in 2026, which the retailer attributed in part to concerns over global uncertainty and potential pressure on food and commodity prices.

FPG may be able to negotiate with suppliers for lower prices or absorb some of the higher costs by accepting lower margins, according to Chua Yeow Hwee, an assistant professor of economics at Nanyang Technological University.

S&P’s team adds that the market leader’s pricing decisions may also exert some competitive pressure on other retailers and keep a lid on price increases in the market.

Still, watchers say the overall impact of such voluntary price controls on inflation is likely limited. 

As a profit-seeking entity, FPG is limited by its own financial resources, despite its social mandate, UOB head of research Suan Teck Kin observes.

The S&P analysts add that such initiatives “cannot fully offset sustained increases in global food, energy, fertiliser or freight costs, particularly given Singapore’s high dependence on imported food”.

Price controls’ high costs

Government price controls may be effective in keeping price rises at bay – to some extent.

At the same time, they can also have unintended negative consequences.

Broad-based price caps and blanket subsidies may benefit not only lower-income households but also affluent ones, resulting in inefficiencies.

Along those lines, the availability of RON95 fuel that is priced significantly below market levels in Malaysia may lead to cross-border leakages, particularly along the Malaysia-Thailand border, according to Gan.

Price controls can also encourage overconsumption. If set below market levels, they may compress margins for producers and retailers, weaken supply incentives and lead to shortages or lower-quality goods.

In Malaysia, cheap sugar has even created tension with public health objectives and burdened the heavily subsidised healthcare system, the S&P analysts remark.

Above all, subsidies come with high public expenditure and, in many cases, become extended drains on state coffers.

S&P estimates that sugar subsidies provided to two refiners in Malaysia, which were initially intended as a stopgap measure in November 2023, now cost the nation RM42 million each month.

NTU’s Dr Chua notes: “(Malaysia’s) fuel subsidy bill is projected to approach RM40 billion in 2026, more than double the amount originally budgeted.”

Lee suggests that the Indonesian government “has had to reprioritise and cut expenditure elsewhere” as a result of commitments not to increase certain fuel prices until the year-end, despite the steep rise in subsidy-related spending.

And although Thailand’s Oil Fuel Fund “looks helpful”, prolonged and pronounced increases in oil prices could mean that the fund’s deficit can widen rapidly, Paracuelles says. That deficit now stands at over 100 billion baht (US$2.98 billion).

If this continues to climb towards 120 billion baht, the government may be pushed to turn to measures such as raising more debt.

“You’re kind of hitting close to that limit already, so I think the response is… try and allow diesel prices to adjust a little bit higher, so (as to) reduce the pressure on the fund,” he says.

Running on fumes

Given that price shocks may be protracted, state-funded price freezes may not be viable in the long term.

Byunghoon Nam, deputy group head and senior economist at Amro, notes that fiscal revenues have generally held up well, on the back of solid economic growth and – ironically – elevated inflation.

“However, borrowing costs are rising, as reflected in higher sovereign bond yields,” he says.

Larger, more persistent energy and food price pressures could increase the strain on public finances and crowd out other spending priorities.

He adds: “Any additional borrowing at elevated interest rates would also raise debt-servicing costs, further limiting fiscal flexibility.”

Says OCBC chief economist Selena Ling: “It’s not just a function of borrowing costs, but also their fiscal position and foreign exchange reserves to sustain those subsidies when global energy or food prices are rising without destabilising their currency, balance of payments or public finances.”

Governments that run fiscal deficits and subsidise prices for certain goods may need to cut back on subsidies or raise new sources of revenue, such as through taxation, she says.

Regional inflation is expected to stay high into early 2027.

“There may be a time lag effect on food prices, even if energy prices stabilise... The risk is for a longer period of elevated and volatile food prices,” says Ling.

The capacity to absorb these prolonged shocks varies by economy. Countries most at risk have large budget deficits, high public debt and sizeable recurring subsidies, as well as current account deficits, reliance on imports, and weak growth, among other factors.

Ling flags economic vulnerability in the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam and India, while Singapore, China, Japan, South Korea and Brunei may be more resilient.

Meanwhile, Malaysia’s state-owned energy company Petronas has recorded “some windfall revenues” on climbing oil prices, which Paracuelles says creates “somewhat of an offset”, as these funds can be tapped by the government to defray subsidy costs.

To keep fiscal outlay sustainable, analysts suggest governments implement targeted and temporary support measures – such as handouts or vouchers as direct offsets, which can be more efficient and more equitable than blanket subsidies – while allowing prices to reflect underlying supply and demand conditions.

Price caps and price-related subsidies can be justified as temporary measures, says Nam, particularly when economic and social stability are at risk. “They can buy time to introduce more targeted support.”

But these should be withdrawn as underlying shocks subside, to reduce the fiscal cost and market distortion, he adds.

In the longer run, improving agricultural productivity, diversifying imports and strengthening supply chains provide more sustainable protection against future shocks, Dr Chua adds.

Sticker shock

Even if price shocks are persistent, subsidies and price caps should be phased out gradually, unless there is a very significant threat to macro-financial stability, Nam tells The Business Times.

He adds that sunsetting subsidies should take place with clear communication from the government to the public, to restore market price signals and contain fiscal costs, while targeted support has to be strengthened for the neediest citizens.

Says Paracuelles: “The way to do it is to have a bit of a medium-term transition plan… obviously you can’t worsen the shock by taking out the subsidies in this period. But at the same time, you also don’t want the subsidies to stay there forever.”

But this may be easier said than done.

“In reality, there are societal pressures and political aims involved as well,” Lee acknowledges. Given ground conditions, “policymakers may not necessarily pursue the most economically efficient way” to temper the impact of inflation.

Letting the cost of living go up is generally unpopular with voters.

Continued fuel subsidies are “partly for political considerations”, Paracuelles says, pointing to upcoming elections in Malaysia, as well as to recent protests by Indonesian students in end-October over issues that included rising prices and dwindling subsidies.

Once price controls are introduced, they can be difficult to unwind, with Gan noting that households and businesses “become accustomed to the support” and Ling pointing to an “entitlement mindset”.

“For domestic sociopolitical (reasons), many governments would still want to be seen as proactively shielding their voters from any sharp inflation shock, especially if it hits essentials like food,” Ling says.

“When you increasingly look around the world and see social protests about cost of living and jobs, policymakers would be under pressure to intervene... maybe the ‘here and now’ matters more for governments facing imminent elections.”

data.title: Issue 221: COP31 goes big on carbon markets; South-east Asia enhances Asean Power Grid agreement
data.description:
Carbon markets

Policy, aggregation lead carbon approaches at COP31

Public-sector support and market aggregation have emerged as two major areas of focus for carbon markets at the annual United Nations climate conference in Turkey.

South-east Asia, with its rich and abundant ecosystems, stands to gain if governments are able to catalyse improved confidence and scale in carbon markets.

The hosts of the climate meeting, known as COP31, had identified carbon markets as a priority issue to better channel capital towards activities that positively impact climate change.

Over the past week, 17 governments endorsed a “policy playbook” that describes eight levers that policymakers can use to enable carbon credit markets at “speed and scale”. The playbook is authored by the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, a group of 18 governments – including Canada, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore and Britain – working to unlock corporate demand for high-integrity carbon credits.

The playbook has a noticeably practical bent, with the policy levers going beyond broad principles to policy actions for countries to implement. The eight levers themselves serve three policy objectives:

  • Support corporate purchases of high-integrity carbon credits;
  • Build buyer confidence and mitigate risk; and
  • Support the development of effective carbon credit markets.

Singapore has also been active on the carbon markets front at COP31.

A Singapore-World Bank partnership known as the Singapore Carbon Markets for Development Programme has released a three-year work plan aimed at helping developing countries to build infrastructure and capabilities to take part in carbon markets.

Singapore authorised the first project aligned with international rules that govern cross-border trading of carbon credits, a clean-water initiative in Rwanda. Preliminary carbon credit deals have also been secured with Kenya and Colombia.

The policy playbook, the cross-border carbon deals and government-driven carbon market initiatives reflect growing government involvement in carbon markets as countries and industries pursue decarbonisation targets, and could provide important tailwinds if supportive policies are put in place.

Another piece of the carbon market puzzle is scale, and aggregation appears to be a favoured solution of the moment.

A Singapore-initiated public-private group called the Action for a Resilient Climate (ARC) coalition – which aims to raise corporate demand for carbon credits – plans to launch its first tender in 2027 to buy a million tonnes of credits.

The policy playbook explains the logic of aggregation. The hypothesis is that pooling demand reduces due diligence costs, supports market building and proofs of concept, and improves the financeability of projects through long-term offtake agreements. Buyers benefit because they can spread risk, improve access and standardise risk management.

Aggregation is being applied on the supply side as well, with project aggregation among the approaches being explored by the Singapore-World Bank programme.

The focus on carbon markets bodes well for South-east Asia, as does the fact that Indonesia, the Philippines and Singapore are part of The Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets. The region continues to face a sizable climate investment gap, which thriving carbon markets can help to close. One estimate by Singapore bank DBS places the region’s cumulative climate investment requirement at US$5.2 trillion from 2025 to 2035 across mitigation, adaptation and resilience areas.

EY notes that South-east Asia accounts for about 30 per cent of the world’s nature-based solutions potential, and has the world’s largest “blue carbon” storage capacity largely due to mangrove areas. Blue carbon projects, in particular, also offer substantial biodiversity benefits. The consultancy estimates that nature-based solutions projects have delivered internal rates of return between 2 and 12 per cent.

A 2025 green-economy report by Bain & Co, GenZero, Google, Standard Chartered and Temasek estimates that South-east Asia’s six largest economies issued about 20 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent credits in 2024, far short of the roughly 720 million tonnes of annual credits from nature-based solutions in those countries.

Singapore, in particular, could potentially reap many benefits. Being an urban, natural resource-limited country, Singapore needs to rely on carbon credits as it progresses towards its climate goals. Furthermore, Singapore has a strategic ambition to be a sustainable finance hub, and thriving carbon markets would be important validation for those plans.

Energy transition

Asean Power Grid is more than a bunch of bilateral deals

South-east Asian leaders have signed an enhanced memorandum of understanding (MOU) on the Asean Power Grid (APG), a regionwide electricity network that was first conceived in 1997 but has made little progress in the 30 years since.

Asean covers 11 countries with very different energy profiles across a vast expanse of land and water, hence difficulty in building a regional power network amid such complexity should not be surprising.

In recent years, Singapore’s pursuit of low-carbon energy imports from its neighbours has fuelled optimism that such imports can spark faster progress on the APG. However, there is a limit to how much Singapore’s energy import projects can advance the APG, because there are fundamental differences between the mostly bilateral, one-way import deals that Singapore is trying to set up and the multilateral, two-way interconnections embodied in the APG’s vision of supporting regional energy resilience.

Some of that complexity is explained in the International Energy Agency’s study into financing the APG. A key observation in the report is that most of the investments in cross-border power projects in South-east Asia have been for one-way power exports, but such investments are insufficient to meet the needs of bi-directional, grid-to-grid projects required by the APG.

Among the APG’s goals are to allow South-east Asian countries to harness complementary energy resources. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ announcement about the latest MOU states that the APG can help to “diversify electricity supplies, improve power system resilience and support renewable energy integration”.

A fee framework that governs how much Singapore will pay for electricity from Indonesia is very different from a two-way agreement that would allow Indonesia to buy electricity from Singapore, much less rules that determine how 11 different countries can trade electricity among themselves. There are also questions involving how capital and operating expenditures related to infrastructure and running the networks should be split, with such decisions taking on a substantially different level of complexity in a multilateral arrangement versus a bilateral one.

The point is that while bilateral deals can help to move progress on the APG forward in certain areas, Asean cannot escape the need to establish a common set of fundamental arrangements across the region as a whole. It will certainly be complicated and challenging, but the struggle will almost certainly be worth it when considering the benefits that a deal could unlock.

Other ESG reads

  • COP31: Singapore to contribute US$500,000 in climate finance to the Pacific islands
  • PM Wong pitches deeper Asean ties on digital payments, energy and haze
  • Malaysia loosens rare earths curbs for France amid upgrade of ties to strategic partnership
  • China’s fossil fuel power tips towards annual drop on green boom
  • Why Singapore should stop trying to recycle everything

data.title: Singapore stocks fall in tandem with regional downturn; STI down 2.1%
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore stocks ended lower on Friday (Nov 20) in tandem with regional declines, tracking overnight losses on Wall Street as Anthropic’s debut on Nasdaq failed to lift the broader market.

The Straits Times Index (STI) lost 2.1 per cent or 104.32 points to finish at 4,975.17. Twenty-six of the benchmark index’s 30 constituents ended the day lower; the remaining four closed flat.

Alvin Lee, premium client manager at IG, said the movement “mirrors the overall risk off sentiment we are seeing across major indices even outside the US, such as the Nikkei and Kospi, which are both down more than 5 per cent”.

“The risk-off sentiment has come from concerns over a hawkish Fed that is widely expected to raise rates even further, with markets pricing in an almost absolute certainty of a rate hike of 25 basis points in December,” he added.

The worst performer among STI constituents was Seatrium , which fell 8.8 per cent or S$0.15 to S$1.56.

CGS International previously downgraded its target price on the counter, a move that Lee said “did no favours to Seatrium’s share price” after a “bearish US session which spread into the STI in general”.

Separately, Seatrium said on Thursday that it expects its FY2026 underlying net profit to be “materially higher” than for FY2025.

The local banks all ended lower on Friday. DBS lost 1.8 per cent or S$1.23 to S$66.11, OCBC fell 3.2 per cent or S$0.88 to S$26.54, and UOB was down 2 per cent or S$0.72 at S$35.42.

Across the broader market, losers beat 493 to 163, after 1.4 billion securities worth S$2.6 billion changed hands.

Key regional indices also ended the day lower.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index lost 1.9 per cent, Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 5.1 per cent, South Korea’s Kospi was down 5.2 per cent and the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI declined 0.6 per cent.

This article was written with the assistance of AI and reviewed by a reporter

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: Mistral AI opens regional HQ in Singapore, seeks to fill 200 roles in Apac
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] French artificial intelligence firm Mistral AI opened its Asia-Pacific headquarters in Singapore on Friday (Nov 20), to host most of the 200 staff that it plans to have in the region by 2027.

The company had around 40 staff in Singapore in May, when CEO Arthur Mensch told The Business Times that it was planning for 100 employees by the end of the year.

Geoff Soon, vice-president of revenue for the Asia-Pacific at Mistral, told BT that Singapore is “not a sales and marketing team”.

“I would say it is about 70 per cent forward deployment capabilities,” he said, pointing out that the company will hire a mix of forward deployment engineers and scientists to fill the Singapore headcount.

He added that Mistral will be looking to hire talents from “leading universities” for these roles.

Forward deployment – a term that has recently gathered pace due to the rise of AI – is the practice of allowing engineers to directly communicate with customers.

Soon said that unlike other tech firms, where engineers typically only fine-tune AI models, the individuals that Mistral recruits will be directly involved in development. “Scientists do the models, the engineers do the agentic capability,” he explained.

Talent is one of the reasons the company set up its regional headquarters in Singapore. Soon noted that the Republic has hosted several multinational manufacturing firms for a long period, giving Mistral an existing talent pool to draw from.

However, he acknowledged that the company will also need to tap people from outside Singapore for roles that workers here cannot fill.

The company will therefore seek to hire an even split of local and international talents. Soon noted that, to this end, Singapore “offers an amazing culture”, which will make it easier to convince people to relocate here.

Speaking as the guest of honour at the opening of Mistral’s office at Asia Square Tower, Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information Tan Kiat How said that having a presence in Singapore is not just about the physical office or headcount.

“It is the capability that grows around it,” he noted, adding that capability can be raised through researchers working on harder problems and engineers gaining exposure and experience with frontier AI models.

Targeting regulated industries

Mistral develops open-source and open-weight large language models. This means that the AI models can run locally on-premises, within company servers, allowing for greater sovereignty and security.

Soon said that the company will, building on its strengths, focus on serving regulated industries such as financial services and the public sector.

Mistral already has a presence in Singapore through partnerships with the Home Team Science and Technology Agency, as well as DSO National Laboratories. The company also has “other customers that are very focused on creating custom models to deliver their sovereign capabilities”.

Asked about his biggest concern about Mistral’s expansion plans, Soon said that more investments need to be made in the digital infrastructure layer. This includes access to more compute such as data centres and chips.

“We need lots of infrastructure,” he added, “to run our experiments and to develop new capabilities as we start to move into longer running agents.”

data.title: Daily Debrief: What Happened Today (Nov 20)
data.description:
Stories you might have missed

‘Chilling effect’: US chips curb could slow down Asean data centre growth; Malaysia, Thailand at higher risk: analysts

[SINGAPORE] Washington’s new curbs on advanced artificial intelligence chips could slow down the next phase of growth for South-east Asia’s data centre build-out, analysts said.

Singapore-based DayOne is said to pause US IPO plans on data centre, market concerns

[HONG KONG] DayOne Data Centres has put plans for its multibillion-dollar US initial public offering on hold, people familiar with the matter said, as investors question the sustainability of frothy valuations for digital infrastructure supporting the artificial intelligence boom.

Indonesia’s PNG supply to Singapore fully restored, no further cuts flagged: METI

[SINGAPORE] Piped natural gas (PNG) supplies from Indonesia to Singapore have been fully restored since Nov 12, nearly three weeks after Indonesia cut exports to the city-state to prioritise domestic consumption.

STI drops below 5,000 points; regional markets also track losses across Wall Street

[SINGAPORE] Singapore fell sharply into negative territory on Friday (Nov 20) morning, tracking overnight losses on Wall Street, where Anthropic’s much-anticipated Nasdaq debut failed to lift the broader market.

‘IPO and beyond’: GIC to stay invested in Anthropic following Nasdaq debut

[SINGAPORE] GIC intends to remain invested in artificial-intelligence company Anthropic beyond its blockbuster initial public offering, as the Singapore sovereign wealth fund looks to deepen its partnership with the Claude chatbot maker.

Singapore, China launch FTA-upgrade talks as leaders discuss closer AI ties

[SHENZHEN] Singapore and China have launched talks to upgrade their bilateral free trade agreement (FTA) to cover new areas such as the digital economy, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on Friday after meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping.

data.title: Soilbuild lawsuit: Brookfield says it moved ahead amid pressure to close S$535.3 million Mapletree deal
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Brookfield Asset Management, accused by Singapore billionaire Lim Chap Huat’s Soilbuild Group of “usurping” a joint venture (JV) deal, expanded on its defence arguments saying it faced “consistent commercial pressure” to close the deal with Mapletree Industrial Trust (MIT).

Lim and Soilbuild had alleged in an action filed on Aug 3 that Brookfield agreed to pursue the acquisition through a JV, and that the two sides worked together for several months on the proposed deal. They claim that Brookfield pulled out of the tie-up two days before Mapletree announced the S$535.3 million sale of the properties to the US asset manager.

In an Oct 20 response to a request for more detail on Brookfield’s defence, the asset manager said: “Mapletree was pressing Brookfield to complete the acquisition of the final seed assets as soon as possible, including by communicating the intended timing for completion and the difficulties in extending Brookfield’s exclusivity period.”

The final seed assets were The Strategy, The Synergy and Woodlands Central. The Strategy replaced 18 Tai Seng in the initial portfolio.

Brookfield gave the account in further particulars of its defence dated Oct 20 seen by The Business Times. The document was served in response to an Oct 6 request for more detail on Brookfield’s defence, including the commercial pressure it said it faced.

It had earlier maintained that it faced “consistent commercial pressures (including from Mapletree) to move ahead with the acquisition expeditiously” so as to maintain the credibility of the interest it had expressed in its letter of intent dated Feb 11, 2025.

In its defence dated Aug 31, Brookfield also said that, despite several rounds of negotiations, “the parties remained in disagreement on multiple key issues” that it considered could not reasonably be resolved. It added that it was “commercially impractical” to delay the purchase indefinitely while awaiting an agreement on the proposed JV.

The US investment giant said its Singapore arm offered S$535.3 million to Mapletree for the revised portfolio in the non-binding letter of intent on Feb 11, 2025.

Brookfield said Mapletree told it on Apr 21, 2025, that it had originally intended the acquisition to take place on May 2, 2025, and was facing “significant pushback” over extending Brookfield’s exclusivity period to May 8, 2025.

It added that Mapletree told it on May 8 that “the acquisition documentation should be finalised as soon as possible”.

On May 15, 2025, Mapletree inquired about the status of the acquisition, and asked whether Brookfield was ready to execute the acquisition documentation that same day, said Brookfield.

“There was also a focus on completing the acquisition of the final seed assets expeditiously including during weekly progress meetings, where Brookfield and other participants in the weekly progress meetings were reminded regularly of the impending expiration of its exclusivity period, and the acquisition timelines,” Brookfield noted.

It told Soilbuild on May 14 that it would proceed with the acquisition on its own.

On May 16, 2025, MIT’s manager announced that sale agreements had been signed for the three properties with buyers managed by Brookfield affiliates. The sale was completed on Aug 15, 2025.

Soilbuild’s claims and Brookfield’s defence 

Brookfield, its Singapore arm and a Brookfield-controlled entity are named defendants in the lawsuit filed with Singapore’s High Court, while Soilbuild’s executive chairman Lim, Soilbuild and a Soilbuild unit are named as claimants.

Lim and Soilbuild are seeking unspecified damages over Brookfield’s alleged breach of an agreement to pursue the JV, as well as the alleged unauthorised use of Soilbuild’s proprietary commercial information, among other claims.

Brookfield denies that the parties had entered into a JV, and said the opportunity to acquire the properties from Mapletree originated from Brookfield. Its Singapore arm submitted its first non-binding offer on Dec 5, 2024, before Brookfield was introduced to the Soilbuild team on Dec 18, it said.

The asset manager added that its Singapore arm and Soilbuild subsequently signed two confidentiality agreements for the initial and revised portfolios.

According to Brookfield, both agreements provided that neither party had “any legally binding obligations to negotiate or consummate the transaction” and that either party could “notify the other party in writing at any time to terminate discussions relating to the transaction”.

It also denied that the parties had agreed on or entered into a memorandum of understanding and that it wrongfully used Soilbuild’s alleged confidential information.

It also denied Soilbuild’s claim that it could not have completed the acquisition without the property group’s involvement.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel Infrastructure Trust,  Elite UK Reit, Thakral, Katrina
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 20):

Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT) : KIT secured S$200 million in revolving loan facilities, with outstanding loans immediately repayable if its trustee-manager ceases to be wholly owned by Keppel Capital and/or Keppel, or ceases to act as KIT’s trustee-manager and a replacement wholly owned by the Keppel companies is appointed beforehand. Neither trigger had occurred yet, but if either leads to cross defaults, about S$1.9 billion in total facilities could be affected. The counter ended 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Thursday, before the news.

Elite UK Reit : The manager of the real estate investment trust (Reit) submitted a planning application for a 352-bed student accommodation development in Wales. It expects a decision in 2027 and aims to start demolition and construction in 2028, subject to approval. The counter ended 1.7 per cent or £0.005 lower at £0.295 on Thursday, before the news.

Thakral : Thakral is selling its remaining 6.1 per cent stake in The Beauty Tech Group (TBTG), netting S$56.5 million, and expects to record a S$17.9 million gain over its end-June book value of S$38.6 million. Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.
